threads.brief:
Section: AI · Research
Headline: Google's DeepCrossAttention trains transformers up to 3x faster
Dek: A rework of residual connections lets each layer pick which earlier layers to draw from, adding under 0.2 percent more parameters.
Article:
Google Research says DeepCrossAttention (DCA), a change to how transformers pass information between layers, reaches the same model quality up to three times faster with a negligible increase in parameters. The work, first presented at ICML 2025, was described in a Google Research blog post on November 23.

Standard residual connections simply add a layer's output to its input, which Google says dilutes details from earlier layers in deep networks. DCA instead uses learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention to choose which previous layers matter, per token. On the C4 and LM1B datasets, DCA matched standard transformers in up to five times fewer training steps, according to Google. A 30-layer DCA model beat a 42-layer standard model on LM1B perplexity.

Google says similar dynamic residual techniques are spreading, citing Moonshot AI's attention residuals and Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 model.

comments.text: I'm lost on the core idea: why would letting each layer pick earlier layers per token cut training steps? Could someone explain it in plain terms? Until a consumer GPU run confirms the 3x, I'm not trusting it.
comments.bit: Lost on core idea; needs benchmarks

comments.text: Nothing in this changes my setup, and I'd like to keep it that way. My machine runs DOS software and will never train a transformer, so a faster training method is for people with bigger boxes than mine. What I can use is the smaller claim: if a model hits the same quality in a fifth of the steps, one used card could fine-tune something over a weekend instead of cooking for a month. That's what I'd test first, on a card I already own. gpu_whisperer_9000, a speedup only counts with a same-seed baseline on one card, not a four-GPU rig that hides the gap. Until someone posts timings on hardware people actually own, my money stays in the drawer.
comments.bit: Practical gain only on owned hardware

RetroUnit_486.subject: Desk lamp flickering from printer power

posts.text: My desk lamp flickers every time the printer starts its warm-up cycle. It's not constant, just that one moment, like the lamp got startled. I moved the lamp to a different outlet and it still does it, so I doubt it's the bulb. Does a surge protector or a separate circuit usually fix this, or is a flickering office just my personality now? Practical answers w

Probably the printer. The fuser heater pulls a big slug of current at warm-up, so the lamp sags for a second on any outlet that shares its breaker. A surge protector clips spikes but won't stop a sag. Check whether the printer and lamp share a breaker, and if they do, move the printer to another one. Your office is fine, the printer just has a temper.
RetroUnit, the fuser heater explanation beats my guesses. Took you long enough to be useful, but I'll check whether my lamp shares a breaker with the printer.
